Low values link to low and high to high, so the correlation across edges is positive, r = 0.774." width="100%"} Measures the tendency of nodes with similar numeric attribute values to connect. Returns the Pearson correlation coefficient of attribute values across edges, indicating whether similar values tend to be connected. Each edge contributes one pair of values (the attribute at each end), and the coefficient is the correlation over all such pairs. Use it to answer questions such as: - do people befriend others of a similar age or income? - do highly cited authors collaborate with other highly cited authors, or with juniors? - are high-traffic nodes linked to other high-traffic nodes (a "rich club" tendency)? For undirected graphs each edge is counted in both orientations, so the result does not depend on which endpoint was listed first. For directed graphs it is the correlation between the source value and the target value of each edge. Every edge counts, including self-loops and parallel edges, and edge weights are ignored. For categorical attributes, use `assortativity_nominal()` instead. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [attribute]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Name of the numeric node attribute to analyze, such as `"age"` or `"income"`. Every node in the graph must have this attribute, and each value must be convertible to a float (integers, floats, and booleans work; strings do not). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Assortativity coefficient in range `[-1, 1]`: - `r = 1`: perfect positive correlation (identical values connect) - `r > 0`: assortative (similar values prefer to connect) - `r = 0`: no correlation - `r < 0`: disassortative (dissimilar values prefer to connect) - `r = -1`: perfect negative correlation ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph has no edges, the attribute is missing on any node, a value isn't numeric, or the values at the edge endpoints have no variance (for example, all equal). ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} For a numeric attribute this reduces to the Pearson correlation between the two endpoint values across every edge. Positive coefficients pick up homophily on the numeric axis (collaborators with similar publication counts, friends of similar ages), while negative coefficients flag structural pairings that link dissimilar values, such as mentor-mentee edges in academic networks or price-inversely-related pairs in economic graphs. The metric assumes the attribute varies across the edge endpoints (a constant attribute produces a $0/0$ division and raises `ValueError`), and it is sensitive to outliers, so running the same computation on log-transformed or rank-transformed values is a common robustness check. The computation is a single $O(V + E)$ pass. ## Examples {.doc-examples} When people mostly befriend others close to their own age, connecting similar numeric values, the numeric assortativity comes out positive (close to 1 here): ::: {#81dd44dc .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_node("Alice", age=25) .add_node("Bob", age=27) .add_node("Carol", age=26) .add_node("Dave", age=55) .add_node("Eve", age=53) .add_edges( [ ("Alice", "Bob"), # Similar ages (25-27) ("Bob", "Carol"), # Similar ages (27-26) ("Dave", "Eve"), # Similar ages (55-53) ("Alice", "Carol"), # Similar ages (25-26) ] ) ) # Returns a positive value: similar-aged people tend to connect g.assortativity("age") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 0.9915397631133672 ``` ::: ::: In academic mentorship networks, senior researchers often collaborate with junior ones, connecting dissimilar values and producing a negative coefficient: ::: {#94bc341f .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_node("Junior1", papers=5) .add_node("Junior2", papers=7) .add_node("Senior1", papers=50) .add_node("Senior2", papers=45) .add_edges([("Senior1", "Junior1"), ("Senior1", "Junior2"), ("Senior2", "Junior1")]) ) # Returns a negative value: experienced researchers connect to juniors g.assortativity("papers") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` -0.9905454545454547 ``` ::: ::: A common use is degree assortativity: store each node's degree as an attribute and measure whether hubs link to hubs. In a star, the hub only connects to leaves, so the result is strongly negative: ::: {#227356ba .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} star = ec.Graph() star.add_star_graph(6) degrees = {nid: star.get_degree(nid) for nid in star.get_node_ids()} star.set_node_attrs("degree", degrees) star.assortativity("degree") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` -1.0 ``` ::: :::
